title: Can data agents do real analysis?
story_key: Shreya Shankar: Can data agents do real analysis? (Data Agent Bench and semantic layers)
summary: In an interview with dbt Labs' Tristan Handy, database researcher Shreya Shankar discusses the Data Agent Bench, a benchmark of AI agents doing junior-analyst work across multiple databases, messy data and free-text columns. The best agent passed 61% of queries on the first try, and agents built on top of a semantic layer did significantly better. The conversation also covers the limits of LLM judges and the lack of good tools for checking agent outputs. This is a researcher's account of an arXiv benchmark, not a peer-reviewed result, and the benchmark details come from the interview rather than the paper.
why_it_matters: It is evidence that a well-maintained semantic model gives agents measurably better accuracy, which supports treating Power BI and Fabric semantic models as the grounding layer for any LLM-based analytics you build.

title: How Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins
story_key: Anthropic: Claude designs scorpion neurotoxin protein binders
summary: Anthropic asked an internal Claude research model to design minibinders, small proteins that attach tightly to a target, against four scorpion neurotoxins. Over about 64 hours it worked mostly autonomously and generated 318,484 designs, and 211 were lab-tested at two contract labs. 17 of them bound their targets, and Anthropic is releasing all 211 designs and their data. The result shows binding only; the team says it has not confirmed that the binders neutralize venom, so no antivenom is claimed.
why_it_matters: It is a concrete, lab-validated example of an agent running a multi-day design campaign end to end, which is useful context for building long-running agentic workflows with Claude, though it is far from your Fabric and Power BI stack.

title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
story_key: Anthropic: LLMs formally verify 100+ open-source libraries at assembly level
summary: Anthropic, with collaborator Theorem, used Claude to produce formal proofs that 123 open-source libraries cannot crash under stated conditions (inputs under 64 MB, single-threaded static RISC-V binary on Linux, fixed memory budget). The proofs turn existing fuzz and test suites into specifications checked at the compiled assembly level, and Claude reportedly found bugs that had survived years of testing. The authors publish a subset of the proofs and a Claude skill for developers, and Theorem offers to run the pipeline on other projects. The work is a company's own report, so the results are not yet independently replicated, and the proofs cover only narrow, stated assumptions.
why_it_matters: If LLM-written proofs become routine, formal verification of critical data-pipeline or parsing code moves from a multi-year expert effort toward something a small team could run, though the practical near-term use is in security-sensitive components rather than BI workloads.

It also lists when subagents still make sense: context bloat, parallel work with fresh context, and tool-selection or instruction conflicts. title: MemCurrent: Designing Persistent Memory for Production Agents

On its own internal benchmark built from Genie conversations (114 test cases), it reports a pass rate of 68.4% versus 22.3% with no memory, and it reports parity with full-context prompting on public benchmarks at about 12x fewer input tokens.
why_it_matters: For anyone building LLM agents on Fabric or Databricks-style stacks, it offers a concrete pattern for combining plugin, tool, and offline-pipeline memory access, but the headline gains come from Databricks' own benchmark and should be treated as vendor-reported until independently replicated.

title: Built for Agents: The Case for Spark Declarative Pipelines
story_key: Databricks: Spark Declarative Pipelines vs procedural PySpark for agent-written pipelines
summary: Databricks benchmarked an AI agent (Opus 4.8) writing 22 data engineering tasks in both procedural PySpark and Spark Declarative Pipelines, with 12 messy input datasets per task (528 builds). Declarative builds were checked by Spark's dry run before execution, which reported about 34x less executor time, about half the code (median 64 vs 131 lines), and fewer in-memory shortcuts, at roughly 2.3x the LLM token cost. The authors also concede that silent logic errors came out level between the two approaches, and the results come from their own benchmark with a public repository.
why_it_matters: If agents are going to write much of your pipeline code, a declarative description that can be validated before execution makes structural mistakes cheap to catch, though it does not remove the need for tests on logic, and the benchmark is vendor-run and Spark-specific.

title: [AINews] Black October

summary: Over roughly 48 hours, a cluster of critical vulnerabilities and breaches was disclosed, including an unauthenticated PHP RCE, a CVSS 10 GitLab flaw, and a LiteLLM 1.107.0 release that shipped with a password stealer. Railway told users to rotate secrets, and Zeabur is shutting down after 321,810 accounts were breached. Microsoft attributes a ConnectWise supply-chain compromise to a China-aligned group that reportedly used an open agentic pentest framework, and the PHP provenance is disputed, with some commentators arguing the disclosures were earlier defensive audits.
why_it_matters: If you build with LLM tooling, check whether LiteLLM 1.107.0 or the other affected packages are in your stack, rotate exposed secrets, and update your pip, uv, certifi and CA store dependencies.

title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here’s Why.
story_key: AI models make progress on open math problems (Erdős unit distance, CDC, Navier-Stokes claims)

It then argues, drawing on W.T. Gowers' commentary, that LLMs search depth-first and can trade compute for time, with an automated verifier pruning failed attempts, so ordinary or implausible hints become cheap to test. Several of the headline claims are cited without source links in the text, so the specific results should be checked before being relied on.
why_it_matters: If verifier-backed, compute-heavy search really works on hard problems, it changes how you should think about pointing LLM agents at difficult analytical tasks: cheap automated checking matters more than the quality of the initial idea.

why_it_matters: If you build Fabric pipelines with Claude or another coding agent, FNTK offers a way to let the agent test code against real data and debug from execution logs instead of copy-pasting results.

It translates eligible Teradata tables, views, procedures, functions and macros, plus SQL and BTEQ code, into Fabric-compatible T-SQL, deploys eligible definitions, and flags scripts that need manual remediation. It does not move the data, which is loaded in a separate step using COPY INTO, pipelines or a copy job.
why_it_matters: If you are scoping a Teradata-to-Fabric Data Warehouse migration, this preview cuts the manual translation work and lets you focus review on exceptions, though validation of data and business logic remains your job.

title: Incrementally migrate and re-migrate database objects with Migration Assistant for Fabric Warehouse (Preview)
story_key: Fabric Warehouse: Migration Assistant incremental migration (Preview)
summary: Microsoft added an incremental mode to Migration Assistant for Fabric Warehouse, now in preview. Users can migrate selected database object definitions (schemas, tables, views) from SQL Server, Azure Synapse dedicated SQL pools, or Teradata in separate runs, and add or re-migrate objects later. Naming conflicts with existing objects are held pending until the user chooses to keep existing, keep incoming, or rename. The tool migrates definitions only and does not synchronize changed rows; data movement is a separate step, for example with a Data Factory copy job.
why_it_matters: If you are moving SQL Server, Synapse or Teradata workloads into Fabric Warehouse, you can now phase the migration by business domain and consolidate into one existing Warehouse instead of creating a new one per run.

why_it_matters: For Fabric teams doing real-time monitoring, it offers a way to build non-standard operational views without a separate front-end build, though it is a preview aimed at a narrow use case.

Operators such as Filter and supported destinations can then take a specific event type as input, with fields limited to that shape.
why_it_matters: If you run Fabric real-time streams with mixed event types, you can filter and route each type using its own fields instead of writing type-guard logic downstream, though the feature is still in preview.

title: How to write AI agent skills
story_key: Tabular Editor: writing AI agent skills
summary: The article explains that an AI agent skill is a folder with a SKILL.md prompt file plus optional reference, script, and asset files, and that it gives the agent context rather than new tools. It argues for progressive disclosure: the always-loaded frontmatter name and description decide whether a skill gets used, while instructions and references load only when needed. It also recommends encoding business processes and definitions rather than technical details, writing skills iteratively from observed agent failures, cutting prescriptive text that confuses the agent, and versioning skills in Git alongside the models they describe.
why_it_matters: For someone building with Claude and Fabric/Power BI, it gives concrete guidance on structuring reusable agent context so the agent triggers the right skill and stays cheap and accurate.
